description: HNOVA is a team of Honduran systems engineers with international experience. We have developed e-commerce, telemedicine, and social platforms for entrepreneurs. In 2025, we were nominated as a Global Team in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. We proudly represent Honduran talent, creating innovative technology with global impact.
summary: Earth Trend Detective is a web application that turns a plain-language question about a place and a period into visual evidence and a statistical answer. A user asks, for example, "How has temperature changed in Tegucigalpa since 2000?"; the assistant interprets the request, the user reviews and confirms it, and the server retrieves the observations from NASA Giovanni (MERRA-2), NASA AppEEARS, or Meteomatics. The app shows monthly and annual series, data coverage, and source provenance and, when at least 10 complete years are available, a linear trend per decade with a 95% confidence interval and a p-value, using ordinary least squares with Newey-West autocorrelation-robust uncertainty. It addresses the four questions of the challenge: what is changing, where, by how much, and whether the change is statistically significant. Users can also compare two locations, two periods, or series from different sessions through seasonally adjusted correlations. This matters because the app separates signal from noise honestly: missing values are never interpolated, insufficient data and provider outages are reported as such, and every number is computed by the server rather than by a language model.
details:
What it does

Earth Trend Detective lets anyone investigate how an environmental variable has changed at a place over time. The user signs in, chooses a workflow, and asks a question in plain English that includes the variable, the location, and the dates. The assistant interprets the request and asks for clarification when needed; the user reviews the proposed request and confirms it before any data is retrieved.

The application offers four workflows. Trend analysis studies temperature or precipitation for one location, compares two locations over common complete years, or compares two periods at one location. NASA Giovanni data queries a curated catalog of NASA Earth science variables for a point and date range. NASA Earthdata explores satellite data from NASA AppEEARS stored as averages over the departments of Honduras. Meteomatics data builds and confirms requests to the Meteomatics Weather API, a separate commercial source that is not NASA data.

How it answers the challenge

What is changing: temperature and precipitation in the trend workflow, plus additional variables in the Giovanni and Earthdata workflows. Where: a geocoded location, two locations, or administrative areas of Honduras, always with coordinates and source context. How much: monthly and annual observations and a linear slope per decade with a 95% confidence interval. Is it significant: a two-sided p-value evaluated at the 0.05 threshold.

How the trend analysis works

The server validates the request, retrieves observations from the selected provider, and builds monthly values. A year is included only when it has 12 valid months. Annual temperature is the calendar-day-weighted mean of the monthly temperatures; annual precipitation is the sum of the monthly totals. Missing values are never interpolated. A linear trend is inferred only when at least 10 complete years and 80% of the requested years are available. The application fits ordinary least squares against calendar years and uses Newey-West autocorrelation-robust uncertainty to report the slope per decade, the confidence interval, and the p-value. Results below the threshold remain descriptive and explicitly report insufficient data.

Comparing sessions

Any result can be compared with a series from another session, for example precipitation in two cities or rainfall against evaporation at one place. Only months where both series have valid values are used. The seasonal cycle is removed by working with monthly anomalies, and the Pearson correlation is reported with a 95% confidence interval and a p-value corrected for autocorrelation through an effective sample size (Bretherton et al., 1999). Spearman correlation, annual and detrended correlations, and lagged correlations are provided as supporting measures. Both series are drawn on one chart, and the aligned values can be downloaded as CSV.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes trend detection accessible to students, journalists, local decision-makers, and curious citizens without programming or statistics software, with a particular focus on Honduras and Central America. Results can be downloaded with their provenance as JSON or saved as a PDF report, so findings can be reproduced and shared.

Factors we considered

Scientific honesty guided the design. A non-significant result does not prove that nothing changed, and a significant trend does not establish its cause; the application says so. Provider outages and missing coverage are reported separately from statistical results, and data from different providers are never spliced together. Each result states its source, coordinates, and coverage.

What makes it creative

The project combines a conversational interface with strict statistical guardrails. The language model never supplies coordinates or numbers: every figure is computed by the server. When the model writes a comparison report, each number in its text is checked against the computed statistics, and any mismatch replaces the text with a deterministic report built from the same values.

Tools and technologies

Interface: React, TypeScript, Vite, MUI, Recharts, and Leaflet. Backend: Firebase Functions v2, Firestore, Firebase Authentication, Genkit, and Vertex AI (Gemini). Data: NASA GES DISC Giovanni (MERRA-2), NASA AppEEARS, Meteomatics, and Open-Meteo geocoding, with an ingestion subsystem that stores multi-source data in PostgreSQL through Prisma.

Use of AI

Gemini is used inside the application to interpret questions and to write qualitative explanations. AI coding assistants were used during development for coding and debugging.
